title: Zach Yadegari on self-belief, skill stacking, and how he sold his app company
summary: Zach Yadegari explains how self-belief and "when, not if" language pushed him toward a teenage revenue goal, and why learning the 20% that matters lets you hire and manage smarter people. He also walks through selling his app company: a lowball first round, a mindset reset, warm intros, and leaning on founders who had sold before.

principles.text: Learn the 20% that delivers 80% of results so you can hire people smarter than you and manage them.
principles.quote: Learn the 20% that gets you the 80% of results. And that's what's necessary to actually hire someone that's smarter than you and being able to manage the team.

principles.text: Self-belief gets you past imagined prerequisites like degrees or classes; assume you can do it now.
principles.quote: I think self-belief has gotten me so far because it's helped me get over so many part points of life where I could have just said like ah like if no one like I have to go to college before I'm able to do this.

principles.text: Shift your language from "if" to "when" even while holding doubts.
principles.quote: I think I've been always conscious about like shifting my language to a when, not an if. Even though I of course I had doubts.

principles.text: Build products from a demand signal you see in the wild, like comments asking for something that doesn't exist.
principles.quote: everyone in the comments was like, "This got me so pumped up. I want to make this my alarm clock. How can I do that?" And there was no way to really easily do that.

principles.text: When selling a company, run a sales cycle: list target buyers and use warm intros to keep leverage.
principles.quote: I made a list of the 10 companies that I felt were made the most sense.

principles.text: In acquisition talks, play hard to get, and lean on founders who have sold before for advice.
principles.quote: What helped me the most was that I had a friend. I actually had a couple people that have been through acquisitions who were I was constantly getting on the phone with them and they were giving me advice throughout the whole process.
